title: Message Queues and Observability
summary: Move slow work out of the request path, then make the whole system visible when something goes wrong.
keyPoints: A queue decouples producers from consumers and absorbs bursts.
A message queue moves events; a task queue adds scheduling and result tracking for background jobs.
At-least-once delivery is the practical default; consumers must handle duplicates.
Retries need backoff, a maximum attempt count, and a dead-letter queue.
Backpressure protects consumers when work arrives faster than it can be processed.
Observability needs metrics, logs, and traces tied together by a request or trace ID.

complexity.note: Task queues add scheduling and result tracking.

commonMistakes: Assuming a queue guarantees exactly-once processing without deduplication.
Retrying immediately and forever, which amplifies an outage.
Letting a queue grow without a plan for backpressure or consumer scaling.
Adding dashboards without alert thresholds or a clear owner.
interviewNotes: Say which work can be asynchronous and which must be synchronous.
For each consumer, state the delivery guarantee and the duplicate-handling strategy.
Name the metrics that would tell you the system is unhealthy, not just busy.
Explain what happens to a failed message after the last retry.

checkYourself.question: Why is at-least-once delivery common?
checkYourself.answer: A consumer can fail after processing but before acknowledging. Redelivery is safer than losing the message, and deduplication handles the duplicate.

checkYourself.question: What is a dead-letter queue for?
checkYourself.answer: It stores messages that exhausted their retries so they can be inspected, fixed, and replayed without blocking the main queue.

checkYourself.question: What is the difference between a metric and a trace?
checkYourself.answer: A metric is an aggregated number over time, such as request rate or error rate. A trace follows one request across services and shows where time was spent.
